newsitem.title: USA: White House sees fast track trade announcement soon.
newsitem.headline: White House sees fast track trade announcement soon.

text.p: The White House said on Thursday that an announcement was imminent on the start of a drive for fast track negotiating authority in Congress with a view to expanding the North American Free Trade Agreement.
White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles told reporters there could be an announcement "shortly" on when the matter would be considered on Capitol Hill.
Bowles said he and others in the Clinton administration were meeting on Thursday and Friday with congressional leaders in order to "attract the broadest possible support."
"Hopefully we will agree on timing; so I would hope you would see an announcement shortly," Bowles said.

Fast track trade authority would allow the administration to negotiate trade agreements without the fear that Congress might later change them. Congress could accept or reject the trade agreements, but could not amend them under fast track.
Clinton wants fast-track trade authority from Congress in order to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) to include Chile, as well as other deals.
The administration has yet to send Congress proposed legislation, saying it is trying to work out a bill that will win bipartisan support.
Bowles said he and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky had met and would continue to meet with members of Congress on this issue, though he acknowledged it could be an uphill fight.
"We believe that we will be able to get fast track authority, we believe it will be a significant battle," Bowles said. "It is something that we're committed to."
That appeared slightly more upbeat than an assessment of prospects for fast track made a week ago by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Rubin told an investment group that getting fast track authority "is going to be very difficult and the odds clearly are not in our favour."
"There are many who believe that NAFTA could not pass (the U.S. Congress) today," Rubin said. NAFTA links Canada, Mexico and the United States in a free trade zone.

Opponents of NAFTA, including some members of Congress and some labour leaders, have complained that the agreement has spawned a rapid rise in the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico, a loss of jobs from manfacturing moving south and lower wages for workers.

But business groups who want to bring Chile into NAFTA and eventually form an Americas trading bloc argue that NAFTA has been good for the U.S. economy and that the United States will be left behind as competitors in Japan and Europe form new trade relationships with Latin American countries, a traditional market for U.S. exporters.

The administration has been without fast track authority since 1994 and efforts to win new trade negotiation legislation have been bogged down in a dispute between Republicans and Democrats over authority to include labour and environmental issues in trade deals.
